  3. Targeted modernization: consolidate when a flow is already being redesigned, or when a capability needs governed exposure to agents.
  4. Automation later: treat AI-assisted migration as something to evaluate once it is a supported capability, not something to plan budgets around today.

I have led enough migrations, from Oracle SOA 11g to 12c, from SOA to SAP BTP and from Boomi to Apigee X, to say this plainly: mass conversions without a business reason rarely pay back. Modernize where the change already touches.

7. Three paths to MCP with the MCP Gateway

This is the part I think matters most for SAP customers. The MCP Gateway in Integration Suite exposes your APIs, integrations and data sources as governed MCP servers. The session described three alternative starting points. They are options, not sequential steps.

Figure 3. Three paths to MCP enablement with SAP Integration Suite.

Path 1: from an API artifact. Expose a deployed API artifact's operations natively as MCP tools. This is the natural route for new API-centric work.

Path 2: from existing API specifications. Bring in specifications from existing API Management deployments or external HTTP endpoints. The technical spec is translated into MCP schema and enriched with natural-language semantics so agents can understand what each tool does.

Path 3: from RFCs. Expose remote-enabled function modules from ECC or S/4HANA. For a lot of customers this is the big one. Many core processes still run on ECC and on BAPIs that have been stable for fifteen years. Rebuilding every one of them as a new REST service before an agent can use it would delay adoption by years. That said, not every RFC should be agent-callable. Pick them deliberately, scope them tightly, and keep the backend authorization checks in place.

Two other points are worth noting. First, SAP Architecture Center now positions the MCP Gateway as the endorsed pathway for external third-party agents and for customer-built agents on BTP to reach SAP systems, with federation of third-party MCP servers on the roadmap. Second, MCP itself is still evolving quickly. If you run self-managed MCP servers, you own the job of tracking the specification and planning upgrades. A managed gateway takes that off your plate, which is a reasonable trade for most enterprise teams.

8. Guardrails are part of the design, not an add-on

In classic integration, it was usually enough to know that application X called API Y. With agents, you need to know which agent acted, on whose behalf, which tool it called, what authorization applied, and whether the business outcome was what everyone expected. Before any agent touches a transactional system, I want to see answers to these:

  • Identity and least privilege. Which agents and users can call which tools? Scoped credentials, not shared master keys.
  • Business authorization. Technical access must never bypass approval limits or segregation of duties. Being able to call submit_for_approval is not the same as being allowed to approve.
  • Input validation. Validate tool inputs against schema and business constraints before anything executes.
  • Traffic management. Rate limits, IP restrictions and payload protection, so a looping agent cannot flood an ECC system.
  • Error semantics. A rejected PO is a business outcome. An unreachable backend is a technical failure. The agent needs to be able to tell the difference.
  • Traceability. Enough logging to reconstruct a tool call end to end during an incident or an audit.
  • Human oversight. High-value or policy-sensitive actions go to a person. Design that path in from day one.

9. Context engineering is an integration concern

There is a common assumption that more context makes an agent smarter. Usually it does the opposite. Twenty overlapping tools and a 4,000-line payload make it harder for the model to choose correctly, and you pay for every token.

What works is focused tool descriptions, explicit input and output schemas, composed responses that contain only what the task needs, and retrieval on demand rather than up front. Notice that almost all of those are decisions made in the integration layer, not in the prompt. How well an agent behaves depends a great deal on what the surrounding architecture lets it see, reach and do.

10. Putting it together: invoice exception management

Here is how I would apply all of this to a scenario most SAP customers will recognize: thousands of supplier invoices a month, most of which match cleanly and a minority that do not.

Routine invoices never see an agent. Integration Suite ingests them, converts formats, runs the deterministic three-way match and posts them according to the rules. There is no reason to pay for reasoning on an invoice that matches.

Exceptions are where the agent comes in. When the match fails on a price variance, a missing goods receipt or a suspected duplicate, the agent calls a composed get_invoice_context tool, compares the evidence, explains the likely cause in plain language and recommends a next step.

Resolution stays controlled. The agent can trigger an authorized action within its limits or route a recommendation to an AP specialist. Either way, the integration layer validates the request and executes it with the normal controls.

Measurement decides whether it was worth it. I would track exception resolution time, the manual intervention rate, integration failure rate, cost per agent invocation and the share of cases resolved within policy. If those numbers do not move, the agent is a nice demo and nothing more.

11. A word on cost

Agent cost is not just tokens. It includes repeated tool calls, orchestration overhead, monitoring, governance and the time people spend investigating odd behavior. Keeping agents off deterministic steps is the single biggest lever. After that: reuse existing iFlows and APIs, keep responses small, compose where it saves calls, and measure consumption next to business outcomes. Edition requirements and AI-unit terms for these capabilities can change, so confirm current details with SAP before you build a business case.

Closing thoughts: orchestration, not universal agentization

The next phase of enterprise AI will not be won by the biggest model. It will be won by the teams that connect models to business processes without giving up the reliability, security and discipline that integration teams have spent years building.

If you are starting this week, here is what I would do:

  1. Take one end-to-end process, such as P2P, and score each step for reasoning value versus execution value.
  2. Pick one exception-heavy step where an agent clearly helps.
  3. Design two or three narrow, composed tools for it. Not twenty.
  4. Expose them through the MCP Gateway using whichever path fits: API artifact, existing spec or RFC.
  5. Put identity, authorization, rate limits and logging in place before go-live, and measure the outcome.

For those of us who have spent our careers in integration, this is good news. The skills that agentic AI needs most (clean contracts, governed access, reliable execution, good observability) are the ones we already have. Our job is not shrinking. It is moving one layer closer to the business.

I would like to hear how others are approaching this. Are you exposing RFCs to agents, or holding back until APIs are cleaner? Let me know in the comments.

entry.title: From SFTP to SFTP: Building a File-Based Integration in SAP CPI
entry.content:
Introduction

File-based integration continues to play an important role in enterprise application landscapes. Even when systems expose APIs, many third-party applications still exchange business data through files, particularly when dealing with bulk records, scheduled transfers, or existing file-based processes.

In this blog, I will walk through my experience of building a file-based integration using SAP Cloud Integration (SAP CPI). The requirement was to receive product information in CSV format from a source SFTP location, transform the data into XML, and prepare the resulting XML file for delivery to a target SFTP directory associated with the SAP application-server landscape.

Rather than focusing only on the configuration steps, I will explain how I approached the requirement, structured the source data, configured the conversion, and validated the resulting XML payload.

1. Understanding the Business Requirement

The requirement was to transfer product information from a third-party system to an SAP-related target environment.

The source system provides product details in a CSV file. The data needs to be processed through SAP CPI and converted into XML before being written to the target SFTP directory.

The integration needed to support the following activities:

  • Poll the source SFTP location for incoming CSV files.

  • Read product records from the source file.

  • Convert the CSV content into XML using the expected XML structure.

  • Transfer the generated XML file to the target SFTP location.

  • Validate that multiple product records are represented correctly in the output.

The target SFTP directory is associated with the SAP application-server directory in the landscape. This relationship is relevant because the generated file is intended to be available to the downstream SAP-side process.

The key objective was to establish a straightforward file-based integration while keeping the transformation and file-transfer responsibilities clear.

2. Understanding the Integration Flow

Before configuring the integration flow, I considered the movement of the file from its source to its destination and identified where the transformation needed to take place.

The high-level process is:

Source SFTP → CSV-to-XML Conversion → Target SFTP

The source SFTP adapter retrieves the incoming file. SAP CPI then processes the CSV payload through the CSV-to-XML Converter. Once the payload has been converted, the target SFTP receiver is responsible for writing the resulting file to the configured destination.

The source polling interval is configured for five minutes, allowing the integration flow to check for incoming files periodically.

This design separates the responsibilities of file retrieval, data conversion, and file delivery. It also keeps the integration flow relatively simple because the current requirement does not involve additional business transformations or XML-to-CSV conversion.

3. Understanding the Source CSV Structure

The next step was to understand the structure of the source file. For this scenario, the CSV contains product information with six fields:

Field Purpose Example :

ProductIDUnique product identifierP1001
ProductNameName of the productLaptop
CategoryProduct categoryElectronics
QuantityAvailable quantity25
UnitPricePrice per unit55000
CurrencyCurrency codeINR

The sample input contains multiple product records:

ProductID,ProductName,Category,Quantity,UnitPrice,Currency
P1001,Laptop,Electronics,25,55000,INR
P1002,Wireless Mouse,Accessories,100,750,INR
P1003,Office Chair,Furniture,15,6200,INR
P1004,Keyboard,Accessories,60,1200,INR
P1005,Monitor,Electronics,20,14500,INR

Working with a clearly defined source structure is important because the CSV-to-XML Converter needs to interpret the incoming columns consistently.

In this configuration, the field separator is a comma. The source file must therefore use comma-separated values in the actual file, rather than relying on visual spacing between columns.

Another important configuration detail is header handling. Since the sample file contains a header row, the converter's header option must be configured and tested appropriately to ensure that the column names are not interpreted as a product record.

4. Defining the XML Structure with an XSD

The CSV data needs a defined XML structure after conversion. To establish this structure, I used an XML Schema Definition (XSD) named Product.xsd.

The schema defines a root element named root, which contains one or more product elements. Each product element contains the six fields from the CSV file.

The intended structure is:

<root>
    <product>
        <ProductID>P1001</ProductID>
        <ProductName>Laptop</ProductName>
        <Category>Electronics</Category>
        <Quantity>25</Quantity>
        <UnitPrice>55000</UnitPrice>
        <Currency>INR</Currency>
    </product>
</root>

The XSD defines the data types for the fields. For example, Quantity uses an integer type, while UnitPrice uses a decimal type. The remaining fields use string types.

Defining the schema helps make the expected XML structure explicit. It also provides a reference for configuring the converter and checking whether the resulting payload matches the intended structure.

For this scenario, the important configuration values are:

  • XML Schema: Product.xsd

  • Path to Target Element in XSD: /root/product

  • Field Separator in CSV: Comma

  • Record Marker: Not specified for this input format

  • Exclude First Line Header: Configure according to the actual CSV header and validate the result

The target element path tells the converter which element represents an individual product record. The schema allows the structure of each product to be represented consistently in the generated XML.

5. Configuring the CSV-to-XML Converter in SAP CPI

With the source format and target XML structure understood, I configured the CSV-to-XML Converter in the integration flow.

The converter is responsible for transforming the incoming CSV payload into an XML representation based on the configured schema and target element.

The configuration involves selecting the XSD, specifying the target element path, and defining the field separator used in the source file.

For this integration, the target element path is /root/product. This means that each product record is intended to be represented as a product element beneath the root element.

The converter configuration needs to match the actual source file. For example, if the file is comma-separated, the configured delimiter must be a comma. Similarly, the header setting needs to reflect whether the incoming file includes a header row.

These settings are important because a mismatch between the source file and converter configuration can lead to incorrectly interpreted records or an unexpected XML structure.

6. Building the Integration Flow

After configuring the converter, I connected it to the source and target adapters in the SAP CPI integration flow.

The main components are:

Source SFTP sender

The sender adapter retrieves the incoming CSV file from the configured source location. The polling interval is set to five minutes.

CSV-to-XML Converter

The converter transforms the CSV payload into XML using the configured XSD and target element path.

Target SFTP receiver

The receiver is configured to write the resulting XML file to the target directory.

The processing sequence is therefore:

  1. The source SFTP location is polled for incoming files.

  2. The CSV file is retrieved for processing.

  3. The CSV-to-XML Converter transforms the product records into XML.

  4. The resulting XML payload is passed to the target SFTP receiver.

  5. The file-transfer result is checked to confirm that the generated XML is delivered to the intended location.

The final validation step is important because successful payload conversion and successful file delivery are separate outcomes. A correctly generated XML payload does not, by itself, prove that the target file has been written successfully.

7. Testing the Integration with Multiple Product Records

After configuring the integration flow, I tested the CSV-to-XML conversion using a file containing multiple product records.

The source file contained five products: a laptop, a wireless mouse, an office chair, a keyboard, and a monitor. Each record had the same six fields, but the values differed by product.

During validation, I checked the XML payload generated by the converter. The output contained the expected root and product structure, with the product details represented as XML elements.

For example, the first product was converted into the following structure:

<root>
    <product>
        <ProductID>P1001</ProductID>
        <ProductName>Laptop</ProductName>
        <Category>Electronics</Category>
        <Quantity>25</Quantity>
        <UnitPrice>55000</UnitPrice>
        <Currency>INR</Currency>
    </product>
</root>

The same structure is intended to be repeated for the remaining product records. In the complete output, each product should appear as a separate product element under the same root element.

This multiple-record test is particularly useful because it checks more than the conversion of a single record. It helps verify that the converter processes repeated records consistently and preserves the relationship between the CSV fields and their corresponding XML elements.

The conversion test was successful: the CSV records were converted into the expected XML structure.

The next validation step is to confirm the complete transfer to the target SFTP directory and verify the delivered file.

8. Validating the Output and File Delivery

Testing a file-based integration should include both payload validation and file-transfer validation.

For payload validation, the important checks include:

  • The XML contains the expected root element.

  • Each source record is represented by a separate product element.

  • The field names match the intended XML structure.

  • The values in the XML correspond to the source CSV values.

  • Numeric fields such as Quantity and UnitPrice are represented correctly.

  • The CSV header is not processed as a product record.

For file delivery, the checks should include confirming that the target SFTP receiver completes successfully, that the XML file is present in the intended destination directory, and that the delivered content matches the generated payload.

Because the target directory is associated with the SAP application-server landscape, confirming the actual file location is also important for downstream processing.

The successful conversion test confirms the transformation stage. The integration should be described as end-to-end successful only after the target delivery has also been verified.

9. File Handling and Reliability Considerations

File-based integrations require attention to more than data transformation. File polling, duplicate processing, archiving, and failure handling can all affect the reliability of the overall process.

For this scenario, the source polling interval is configured for five minutes. The behaviour of the source adapter when a file is read, processed, or encountered again should be understood as part of the overall design.

Depending on the business requirement, additional considerations may include:

  • Duplicate processing: Ensure that the same input file is not unintentionally processed multiple times.

  • Archiving: Retain processed source files when required for traceability or auditing.

  • Failure handling: Establish how failed conversions or unsuccessful target transfers will be identified and investigated.

  • File naming: Ensure that the generated XML file has an appropriate name and extension for the receiving process.

  • Monitoring: Review the integration message processing status and relevant logs when validating the flow.

These are reliability considerations rather than claims that every feature has already been implemented in this integration. Any archive, retry, exception-handling, or duplicate-prevention behaviour should be documented according to the actual configuration and test results.

Considering these aspects early helps make a simple file transfer more dependable when it is used in a production landscape.

10. What I Learned from This Implementation

This implementation reinforced several practical points about developing file-based integrations in SAP Cloud Integration.

Understand the source data before configuring the converter. Knowing the delimiter, field order, and header format makes it easier to configure the conversion correctly.

Keep the XML structure explicit. The XSD and target element path help define how individual records should be represented in XML.

Test with multiple records. A successful single-record conversion is useful, but testing several records helps validate repeated element generation and data consistency.

Separate transformation testing from delivery testing. A correct XML payload demonstrates that the conversion works. The target receiver must also be verified to establish that the file reaches its destination.

Treat file handling as part of integration design. Polling behaviour, file naming, duplicate prevention, monitoring, and failure handling should be considered alongside the transformation itself.

These lessons apply to other file-based integration scenarios in which data moves between external systems and SAP-related environments.

Conclusion

In this implementation, I built a file-based integration flow in SAP Cloud Integration to receive product information from an SFTP source, convert the CSV data into XML using an XSD-based configuration, and prepare the generated XML for delivery to the target SFTP directory.

The multiple-record conversion test confirmed that the source product data could be represented using the expected XML structure. This provided a useful validation point before completing the checks for target file delivery.

For me, the exercise highlighted how a clearly defined source format, a consistent XML schema, and focused testing can simplify the development of a file-based integration.

Although the flow is straightforward, validating each stage separately—from file retrieval and conversion to final delivery—is essential to establishing confidence in the integration.

I hope this walkthrough helps others who are building similar file-based integrations using SAP Cloud Integration.

entry.title: BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent | Part 4: Switching on Transport and the first transport
entry.content:
Part 4 of the series BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent.

In Part 3 we finished the receiving end in Central. All the pipes are in place. In this part we give the right person the right role, switch on Transport in Integration Suite, check every connection, and send the first package all the way to the target.

Step 1: Give yourself the transport role

Up to now every role went to a service instance. Clicking Transport is done by a person, so this one goes to a user.

  • In the Dev subaccount, go to Security > Role Collections and create a role collection, for example CPI-Transport.
  • Add the role WorkspacePackagesTransport and assign the collection to everyone who should be able to transport.
  • The same users also need the normal Integration Suite role collections (for example PI_Integration_Developer, and PI_Administrator for the settings in step 2).

After assigning roles, log out and in again or reload the browser tab. The old login does not know about the new role.

Step 2: Switch on Transport in Integration Suite

In the Dev Integration Suite, go to Settings > Integrations > Transport, choose Edit, set Transport Mode to Transport Management Service and save. Then choose Check Configuration. It tests the destinations from Part 2 and should end with success.

Step 3: Check the connection in Content Agent

Open the Content Agent UI (subscription) in Dev and go to Cloud Transport Management Service. With destination TransportManagementService selected, the status must say Connected, and you can pick the source node from Part 1. This is the check that catches wrong credentials, which Check Connection in the cockpit does not.

 

The same screen in my setup, before and after fixing the client ID.

Step 4: Send the first package

In Integration Suite, open a small test package under Design and choose Transport. Add a short comment and confirm. Integration Suite hands the package to Content Agent, Content Agent packs it, and the parcel lands at the source node and moves along the route to the target node.

Use a package with one simple iFlow for the first run. If something fails, you want the problem to be the setup, not the content.

Step 5: Import in CTMS

Open CTMS, go to the target node and open its import queue. Your transport request is waiting there. Select it and choose Import. CTMS hands the parcel to the second Content Agent through CAS_on_target, which writes the package into the target Integration Suite. When the status shows success, open the target workspace: the package is there.

The person who imports needs the CTMS role ImportOperator in a role collection (see the roles table in Part 1).

What tripped me up in my setup

  • Transport Mode stayed greyed out. I spent a long time on the wrong things: which runtime instance, which key, which destination. The real cause was simple: WorkspacePackagesTransport was not in the custom role collection I had assigned to my user in Dev. Once I added it, Transport Mode could be set. If this option is disabled for you, check the user's role collections first.
  • Integration Suite did not open properly in Dev. The Integrations area was not visible until I assigned the normal Integration Suite role collections (PI_Administrator, PI_Integration_Developer, PI_Business_Expert, PI_Read_Only) to my user. The transport role alone is not enough.
  • Check Configuration failed with a token error. My first check ended with "Failed to fetch auth token(Destination Name: ContentAssemblyService)". The useful part is the destination name at the end: it tells you exactly which of the three destinations cannot log in. Compare that destination's client ID, client secret and token URL (including /oauth/token) with its service key.
  • Content Agent said "Not Connected". The screenshot above is from my setup. The TransportManagementService destination looked fine in the cockpit, but its client ID did not match the CTMS key. After fixing it, the status changed to Connected.

What comes next

Integration packages now travel from Dev to Central. In Part 5 we use the same setup to transport something different: role collections.

entry.title: Pipeline for Cloud Integration: Exactly Once In Order routing for XI and IDoc inbound processing
entry.content:
In the newest version of the Pipeline for Cloud Integration, we added Exactly Once In Order (EOIO) routing directly into the inbound processing step for both XI and IDoc — the two protocols where ordered delivery matters most in SAP-to-SAP integration. When a message arrives flagged as EOIO, the pipeline detects this at the earliest possible stage and routes it on a dedicated route — bypassing the pipeline steps that are currently incompatible with ordered processing today — and forwards it either to an exclusive JMS queue or a ProcessDirect endpoint. See In Order Handling.

It was a conscious decision not to support EOIO in the pipeline right now as long as we do not support dynamic serialization context which - once supported - will give us much more flexibility in handling EOIO scenarios. So, the current delivery does not cover an End-to-End scenario for EOIO but is a first step to unblock customers that are requiring this and want to use the generic IDoc and Proxy inbound.

You configure the EOIO routes in the Partner Directory for the partner ID representing your configuration scenario. For this, the string parameter InOrderRouteOption has been introduced. As value of the parameter, you need to specify the route option and its specifics. The following options are supported:

  • You route the EOIO messages to an exclusive queue which name is based on the sender context.
  • You route the EOIO messages to an exclusive queue with a name chosen in the Partner Directory.
  • You route the EOIO messages to a ProcessDirect endpoint.

If nothing has been configured, EOIO messages will fail in the generic XI and IDoc inbound processing flows with custom status ConfigurationOptionNotSupported.

In either case, you need to create an integration flow where you implement the In Order settings on your own. For the ProcessDirect option, you directly send the EOIO message synchronously to the integration flow. When choosing the exclusive queue option, you decouple the generic XI and IDoc inbound processing flows from your integration flow. By persisting the messages in a JMS queue, Cloud Integration can carry out the retry of the message delivery if there's an error. Because an exclusive JMS queue can have only one consumer at a time, the message sequence can be preserved. See Quality of Service Exactly Once In Order.

In the following, let's go through the different options.

Exclusive queue based on sender context

For XI messages sent with Quality of Service Exactly Once In Order, the XI sender adapter sets the message headers SapQualityOfService equals ExactlyOnceInOrder and SapQueueId holding the queue ID of the incoming message. For the IDoc sender adapter, the message headers SapPlainSoapQoS and SapPlainSoapQueueId are set based on the IDoc control header ARCKEY. Your EOIO messages can then be routed to an exclusive queue with a name provided in the headers SapQueueId and SapPlainSoapQueueId, respectively.

Create an integration flow with an exclusive JMS sender queue. As name for the exclusive JMS sender queue choose the name of the queue ID sent with the message. If different queue IDs are sent, you need to create multiple integration flows. As you can see, this doesn't scale unlimited. So, this only works for quite static queue settings.

In the Partner Directory, maintain the partner ID representing the configuration scenario. Create the string parameter InOrderRouteOption with value ExclusiveQueue:UseSenderContextAsQueue.

Exclusive queue with configured name

Like in the option before, you can use an exclusive JMS queue to decouple the generic XI and IDoc inbound processing flows with from your integration flow. Here, however, you can give the exclusive queue an own name.

Create an integration flow with an exclusive JMS sender queue. As name for the exclusive JMS sender queue choose the configured name, here PIP2EOIO, see below.

In the Partner Directory, maintain the partner ID representing the configuration scenario. Create the string parameter InOrderRouteOption with value ExclusiveQueue:<your chosen queue name>, in this example ExclusiveQueue:PIP2EOIO.

Optionally, because we bypass the rest of the pipeline, in particular the receiver determination, you can create a string parameter receiverDetermination with value equals the receiver system name. Another option would be to create a message header SAP_Receiver in the integration flow holding the receiver system name. This is actually supported for all options, but not shown in the other screenshots.

ProcessDirect option

You can route the EOIO message to an integration flow which you synchronously call via ProcessDirect adapter. In this case, create an integration flow with a ProcessDirect sender adapter.

In the Partner Directory, maintain the partner ID representing the configuration scenario. Create the string parameter InOrderRouteOption with value ProcessDirect:<your chosen ProcessDirect end point>, in this example ProcessDirect:/PIP/Step07/Samples/Scenario_2/EOIO.

 

Special use case: XI to XI route-through

Let's take a look at a special use case. We like to achieve EOIO delivery for a route-through scenario with XI sender and XI receiver, i.e., Point-to-Point without mapping. In this case, we can actually apply the ProcessDirect option whereas as ProcessDirect In Order route we choose the end point of the generic XI outbound processing flow. So, the generic XI inbound processing flow directly calls the generic XI outbound processing flow. The headers SapQualityOfService and SapQueueId are passed through. This ensures that the XI receiver adapter calls the receiver system in Exactly Once In Order mode. Furthermore, dynamic queue IDs are supported. Note, that in this case, the restart in case of a message failure is handled by the sender system.

In the following, we go through the configuration in detail. The colour coding is defined as follows: Green has to do with the landscape staging settings and the partner ID determination, Blue refers to the In Order routing, and Red refers to the XI outbound settings. First of all, we need a partner ID representing the sender system alias with an alternative partner that maps the actual sender business system to the sender system alias. In this case, we assume that we run the scenario in the QA landscape. For an incoming message, the business system is mapped to the alias. Within the pipeline, we work with alias.

Next, for the partner ID representing the configuration scenario we define an alternative partner that maps the sender system alias, the sender interface name and the sender interface namespace to the configuration scenario. This way, we determine the configuration scenario based on the incoming message.

On the String Parameters tab, we define how the configuration scenario is configured. The string parameter receiverDetermination defines the receiver system alias. The InOrderRouteOption defines how we handle the In Order processing. In this case, we opt for the ProcessDirect option. As mentioned above, as address we maintain the end point of the generic XI outbound processing flow. Furthermore, we define the settings of the XI outbound processing, in this case the receiver interface name and its namespace. See XI Receiver Adapter.

For the receiver system alias, we also need to define an alternative partner that maps the actual receiver business system to the receiver system alias. Before we send out the message to the receiver, we map the alias to the corresponding business system.

For configuring the XI connection parameters, we support different options. In our case, we use the Partner Directory option. For this, we create a partner ID representing the actual receiver business system and maintain the configuration parameters. i.e., proxy type, authentication type, credential name, and XI end point of the receiver system. For a complete list of configuration options, see XI Receiver Adapter.

If you run the scenario, you should see two message processing logs in the message monitor belonging to one message exchange. As you can see, the message has been routed through and delivered via Exactly Once In Order.

The options outlined here are initial steps to realize EOIO extending the generic XI and IDoc pipeline steps. We are looking into options to realize the E2E scenario using Exclusive Queue but also the planned "Support many serialization contexts for parallel exactly once in order processing (EOIO)" via the pipeline. Therefore, please stay tuned for further updates of the pipeline package.

entry.title: Integration Advisor – RosettaNet PIP Messages
entry.content:
I am happy to share the latest update to the B2B offerings of Integration Advisor and Cloud Integration (part of SAP Integration Suite): the RosettaNet Message Standard is now supported. In this blog post, I will give you a brief overview of this message standard and explain how to use it.

RosettaNet Library in Integration Advisor

This new B2B library consists of the so-called RosettaNet Partner Interface Processes (PIPs), specified for the high-tech industry. This standard was originally owned by the RosettaNet consortium and later became part of the GS1 US organization.

Our offering includes a total of 269 messages across 104 distinct PIP codes. See the screenshot below for an example of the Messages list in Integration Advisor.

Our content is based on the original RosettaNet specifications previously published on the GS1 US website. Note that this content was removed from the GS1 US webpage earlier in 2026.

More specifically, we considered the PIP specifications for the 01, 02, and 03 version series. RosettaNet had also begun converting some of the PIP specifications into a newer XSD-based format, published as the V11 series. The content of this V11 series is currently not available in Integration Advisor, as it was not part of SAP Process Integration and SAP Process Orchestration (SAP PI/PO) and we have not received any reports of customers using this newer format. Please contact us (e.g. via a comment on this blog post) if you require the V11 series. Based on demand, we can add it to Integration Advisor at a later stage.

One additional background note: RosettaNet distinguishes between the following version status types for a PIP version: Draft (D) → Beta (B) → Release (R) → Validated (V), where V represents the final state. The majority of the offered PIPs (216) are in the Validated state (e.g. PIP3A4_V02_02_PurchaseOrderRequest). In addition, GS1 US listed a number of PIPs (53) in the Released state (e.g. PIP2C7_R01_00_BillOfMaterialConfirmation). Based on our interpretation, these PIPs were released and used productively but were never advanced to the final Validated state, and were therefore listed with their last known status. For two specific PIPs (PIP2C9 and PIP3B11) GS1 US listed content for both R and V states, and we have followed this approach in Integration Advisor. Please note that no content considered work-in-progress (i.e. Draft or Beta states) is offered.

Versioning of RosettaNet Messages

RosettaNet versioned all messages separately and published updates for each message independently. This means there is no concept comparable to a release version as known from many other B2B standards (such as 004010 for ASC X12, D.01B for UN/EDIFACT, or 1.2.065 for cXML). 

For example, in the screenshot above, PIP3A4_V02_02_PurchaseOrderRequest represents version V02.02 of the PurchaseOrderRequest message (PIP code PIP3A4). For some message types, multiple versions were published (e.g. 9 versions for PIP4C1 or 7 versions for PIP3A4), while other message types have only a single version (e.g. PIP3A13 or PIP4A1). 

Due to this versioning strategy, and given that no further updates to RosettaNet messages are expected, all definitions are grouped in Integration Advisor into a single version called All. This version contains 267 message types. 

Moreover, the RosettaNet standard didn't define reusable Codelists, Complex Types, or Simple Types. Therefore, no explicit content is provided in the corresponding sections in Integration Advisor. However, the Codelists, Complex Types, and Simple Types are implicitly part of the RosettaNet message types and frequently exhibit similar details across different message types.

Additional Semantic Details for RosettaNet Messages

In Integration Advisor, we always strive to go beyond the pure technical specification of a B2B library. We provide additional semantic details inline and out of the box. These include, for example, documentation, allowed code values, and value specifications (via data type, length, and representation).

The RosettaNet standard technically specified the RosettaNet PIP messages based on the older schema definition language DTD. Such DTDs do not include additional semantic details such as documentation or value specifications. All values are assumed to be of type String, and no length information is available. This is why other mapping tools such as SAP Process Integration and SAP Process Orchestration (SAP PI/PO) do not offer semantic details for RosettaNet.

In addition, RosettaNet published so-called Message Guidelines (in HTML format), which included more semantic details such as documentation, code values with descriptions, and details for Simple Types including length and representation.

In the Integration Advisor offering, the technical DTD specification and the semantic HTML guideline details are combined to provide a holistic view of all the details of a RosettaNet PIP message. For an example, see the screenshot below.

Besides adding semantic details, the RosettaNet HTML guidelines also permit certain deviations from the actual message structure, such as deselecting optional elements or restricting cardinality. When preparing the content for Integration Advisor, we decided to keep the PIP message structure in line with the technical DTD specification and to use the HTML guidelines solely for enriching semantic details.

Special attention was given to the appropriate representation of data types and their properties. The following table provides more details on how the RosettaNet data types are represented in Integration Advisor.

RosettaNet used the concept of Representation to further specify the allowed value space. For example, the representation 9(9)4(X) (for Global Location Identifier) means that (up to) 9 digits are followed by (up to) 4 characters (e.g. 123456789ZZZ). In Integration Advisor, the Representation (where specified by RosettaNet) can be found in the details area for a node, under the Notes tab.

A few things to note regarding the representation of three Global Identifiers in the RosettaNet content:

  • Global Business Identifier
    • The GlobalBusinessIdentifieridentifies a business and is specified via the DUNS number.
    • RosettaNet defines this entity as type Integer with length [9..9] and the representation 9(9).
    • In XSD, it is not possible to use the primitive type xsd:integer for this, as it does not allow the minLength=9 constraint to be expressed appropriately.
    • Therefore, we have chosen the XSD primitive type xsd:token together with length [9..9] and the additional XSD pattern \d+ (to ensure that only digits are permitted).  
  • Global Location Identifier
    • The GlobalLocationIdentifierdescribes a location uniquely identified by the DUNS+4 number.
    • In the majority of PIPs this entity is specified as type String with length [10..13] and the representation 9(9)4(X). However, a number of PIPs incorrectly use type Integer. 
    • In Integration Advisor, we consistently use type String together with length [10..13].  
  • Global Product Identifier
    • The GlobalProductIdentifier specifies a product identified by the Global Trade Identification Number (GTIN).
    • RosettaNet consistently defines this entity as type String with length [14..14] and the representation 9(14).
    • We represent this entity as type String together with length [14..14] as well, and include the representation 9(14) as part of the documentation. However, we have not added the additional XSD Pattern \d+ by default. (Unlike the Global Business Identifier, RosettaNet uses type String here, so we were not entirely sure whether the intention was to keep the option open for non-digit characters.)
    •  If you want to enforce that only digits shall be permitted, you can easily add the XSD pattern \d+ in your MIG. 

RosettaNet uses special date/time conventions, such as 20260618T114000.000Z. These are very similar to the standard XSD date and/or time conventions but differ in that hyphens and colons are omitted. We have included three additional Date Time Formats specific to RosettaNet and automatically assigned these patterns to the corresponding fields: pattern CCYYMMDD'T'hhmmss'.'fffZ for DateTimeStamp, pattern CCYYMMDDZ for DateStamp, and pattern hhmmss'.'fffZ for TimeStamp. In addition, we have added two more Date Time Formats to accommodate optional parts: pattern CCYYMMDD'T'hhmm[ss['.'fff]][Z] for DateTimeStamp (specified with length [13..20]) and pattern hhmm[ss['.'fff]][Z] for TimeStamp (specified with length [4..11]).

There is one minor limitation to note for FreeFormText: This field is specified with Min Length = 1 (but without Max Length) in the RosettaNet HTML Guidelines. In Integration Advisor, however, FreeFormText > CONTENT has no Min Length assigned to it.  (The reason for this is that FreeFormText is a so-called XSD Simple Content, which does not allow length specifications to be added without further modification of the XSD structure.) If this Min Length value is important for your use case, you can simply add it in your MIG. 

RosettaNet Usage in SAP Cloud Integration

Cloud Integration now supports the processing of RosettaNet messages. You can use the RNIF (RosettaNet Implementation Framework) adapter to exchange RosettaNet business messages with trading partners over HTTPS, in compliance with the RNIF 2.0 specification. The adapter supports both sender (inbound) and receiver (outbound) channels. For more information, refer to the Online Help.

For the runtime, one minor technical point is worth mentioning. Many RosettaNet payloads include a DOCTYPE declaration (such as <!DOCTYPE Pip3A4PurchaseOrderRequest SYSTEM "3A4_MS_V02_02_PurchaseOrderRequest.dtd">) at the beginning of the XML payload. The purpose of this is to allow payload validation against the underlying DTD schema. Integration Advisor and Cloud Integration, however, work with the newer XSD schema definition language. Such a DOCTYPE declaration does not interact well with XSD schema processing (e.g. in the XML Validator flow step). Therefore, DOCTYPE declarations are not part of the Integration Advisor processing and are automatically removed from the payload if present.

In Integration Advisor, each RosettaNet Message or MIG includes, for your reference, a documentation note (on the Notes tab) with the DTD file name (e.g. Original DTD file name: 3A4_MS_V02_02_PurchaseOrderRequest.dtd). This can be helpful if your business partner expects the DOCTYPE declaration to be set.

Conclusion

With this latest update, we now support the RosettaNet Message Standard. You have an end-to-end solution that allows you to view and customize RosettaNet messages in Integration Advisor and send and receive these messages in Cloud Integration.
